limitations: As a field study, it was impractical to counterbalance the order of the four lamp types in order to avoid potential order bias.
The participants completed EMAs 10 times, but only completed the web-based surveys once under each treatment condition, suggesting EMAs have higher reliability.
The reason for the significance of LB23 (a lighting belief question) is not clear and merits further investigation.
The study's findings regarding 5000K conditions being uncomfortable for those with daylight access merit further investigation.
minimum_safe_summary: This field study investigated the effects of correlated color temperature (CCT) and lumen output of fluorescent lighting on office workers' visual comfort, brightness perception, satisfaction, and self-reported productivity. Twenty-six participants experienced four luminous conditions (3500K/2330lm, 5000K/3000lm, 3500K/3000lm, 5000K/2330lm) over three months, providing responses via ecological momentary assessments (EMAs) and web-based surveys. Key findings indicate that while 5000K CCT (cooler) was rated brighter, especially with higher lumen output, this came at the cost of lower satisfaction, worse visual comfort, and reduced self-reported productivity. 5000K conditions were perceived as 'too cool,' particularly by occupants with daylight access, and led to increased glare on computer screens. The study concludes that the U.S. Department of Energy's spectrally enhanced lighting (SEL) method, which advocates for higher CCT to save energy, compromises occupant comfort and satisfaction, and its claims about spatial brightness perception are not generalizable. A limitation was the inability to counterbalance lamp type order in the field setting.
